why: the route through disp leaves owner-only vs any linked person to be decided, and neither the question nor the documentation supports the unfiltered choice: the district choice is coupled to an unsupported role choice

revision.decision: Which district counts as the branch where the client opened their account: the client's own district (client.district_id) or the account's branch district (account.district_id).
revision.reading_B: Count female clients who are linked to at least one account whose branch district (account.district_id) is Jesenik. Each client is counted once, and the client's own district is ignored.
revision.sql_B: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.client_id) FROM client AS T1 INNER JOIN disp AS T3 ON T1.client_id = T3.client_id INNER JOIN account AS T4 ON T3.account_id = T4.account_id INNER JOIN district AS T2 ON T4.district_id = T2.district_id WHERE T1.gender = 'F' AND T2.A2 = 'Jesenik'

edits.edit: Add INNER JOIN disp AS T3 ON T1.client_id = T3.client_id and INNER JOIN account AS T4 ON T3.account_id = T4.account_id
edits.why_required: account.district_id can only be reached from client through the disp bridge table, because the schema has no direct link from client to account.

edits.edit: Change the district join from T1.district_id = T2.district_id to T4.district_id = T2.district_id
edits.why_required: This is the choice itself: the Jesenik filter must test the account's branch district, not the client's own district.

The disp/account join can return a client more than once if they are linked to several Jesenik accounts. Reading A counts each client once, so B must remove those duplicates to keep the same unit of counting.

revision.note: Going through disp forces a disp.type decision: either filter the role (for example type = 'OWNER') or leave it unfiltered. No neutral option exists. Leaving it unfiltered is the smallest change, because it adds no filter that A lacks: A counts every female client whatever their disp role, and B does the same, changing only where the district is read from. Adding type = 'OWNER' would be a real second choice layered on top ('opened' meaning the account owner), which gives C0 = 22. So owner-only belongs in its own separate record, not in B. The recorded SQL B is already the minimal version of the district choice and stays unchanged. The part that cannot be removed is the unfiltered disp join, which exists only because the account's district is reachable only through disp.

why: opus: ["Which district_id defines a customer's 'Prague branch': the district of the accounts they hold (account.district_id via disp) or the client's own district (client.district_id)"]; sonnet: ["Which branch-location column defines 'Prague branch': client.district_id (the client's own district) versus account.district_id (the account's branch district).", "Whether the population must be restricted to clients who actually have accounts (via disp), or includes any client in the district regardless of account linkage.", "Deduplication: R2 counts each client once even if linked to multiple Prague accounts, while R1 does so implicitly since it has one row per client (this follows from the other choices rather than being independent)."]

revision.decision: Which district link defines a customer 'at the Prague branch': the client's own district (client.district_id) or the branch district of the account the client holds (account.district_id reached through disp).
revision.reading_B: Customers at the Prague branch are the clients linked through disp to at least one account whose branch district is in the Prague region (account.district_id -> district.A3 = 'Prague'). The result is the share of those clients who are female, counting each client once, just as the gold does.
revision.sql_B: SELECT CAST(SUM(T2.gender = 'F') AS REAL) / COUNT(T2.client_id) * 100 FROM client AS T2 WHERE T2.client_id IN (SELECT T4.client_id FROM disp AS T4 INNER JOIN account AS T3 ON T4.account_id = T3.account_id INNER JOIN district AS T1 ON T3.district_id = T1.district_id WHERE T1.A3 = 'Prague')

edits.edit: Replace the direct join client.district_id = district.district_id with a membership test: client_id IN (clients linked through disp to an account whose account.district_id belongs to a district with A3 = 'Prague').
edits.why_required: This is the choice itself. Under reading B, the Prague condition applies to the account's branch district, which can only be reached through disp and account, not through the client's own district_id.

edits.edit: Express the new path as a semi-join (IN subquery) and do not join disp and account into the outer FROM clause.
edits.why_required: A client can have several disp or account rows. A plain join would count such a client more than once. The gold's unit is one row per client, because client -> district is many-to-one. The semi-join keeps that unit without changing the aggregate, so SUM(gender = 'F') / COUNT(client_id) stays exactly as in the gold.

revision.note: The recorded SQL B made two changes: it moved the Prague condition onto account.district_id, and it rewrote the aggregates to COUNT(DISTINCT CASE ...) / COUNT(DISTINCT client_id). The aggregate rewrite can be removed. The gold already counts each client exactly once, so keeping that unit is not a second interpretation choice. The account path, however, needs some way to avoid counting a client more than once, and a semi-join does this while leaving the gold's aggregate unchanged. In the standard Berka data each client has only one disp row, so deduplication probably makes no numeric difference, and most or all of the 48.87 vs 49.78 gap probably comes from the district-link choice. I did not check this against the database.

why: opus: ["Output granularity: one label per patient (GROUP BY ID) or one label per lab record", "How to combine a patient's multiple lab records into one label: 'normal' only if all records are in range (MIN), rather than any record, the latest record, or an average ALB"]; sonnet: ["Output granularity: one row per lab record (R1) versus one row per patient (R2).", "Aggregation rule for collapsing a patient's multiple records into one label: 'normal' only if every record is normal (R2's MIN). This rule is only needed once you choose per-patient output, and other rules such as latest record or any normal record would also be possible."]

revision.decision: Granularity of the output: one normal/abnormal label per Laboratory record, or one label per patient born in 1982 ('their albumin').
revision.reading_B: Output one label per patient born in 1982 instead of one per lab record. Each patient's label comes from the gold's own per-record test: the patient is 'normal' only if every one of their Laboratory records would get 'normal' from the gold CASE. A NULL ALB still counts as 'abnormal', as it does in the gold.
revision.sql_B: SELECT CASE WHEN MIN(CASE WHEN T2.ALB >= 3.5 AND T2.ALB <= 5.5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1 THEN 'normal' ELSE 'abnormal' END FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', T1.Birthday) = '1982' GROUP BY T1.ID

edits.why_required: This is the choice itself: it gives one output row per patient instead of one per Laboratory record.

edits.edit: Keep the gold's per-record CASE test unchanged, map it to 1/0 inside an aggregate (MIN(...) = 1), and turn that result back into the 'normal'/'abnormal' label
edits.why_required: Once rows are grouped, the per-record labels must be combined into one label. Wrapping the gold's exact test keeps its range bounds and its NULL→'abnormal' behaviour. By contrast, MIN(ALB)/MAX(ALB) skip NULLs, so a patient with some NULL results and otherwise in-range values would wrongly come out 'normal'.

revision.note: Only part of the reviewer's point can be removed. The change in NULL handling was not part of the choice and can be removed: this sql_B treats a NULL ALB as 'abnormal', exactly like the gold. Some rule for combining a patient's records cannot be removed, because the per-patient reading needs one. I used 'all records normal' because it reuses the gold's per-record test unchanged and adds no new threshold or ordering logic. Using the most recent value would add a separate choice (a Date ordering or subquery). Per the reviewer's data, only one patient was born in 1982, so the output drops from 35 rows to 1.
